notes:
Here are the notes on Genesis 41:1–28. Every point comes from a page I actually read, and the URL follows each point. A few gaps up front:

- **Not found:** anything from newadvent.org, catholic.com or oca.org (Catholic and Orthodox), any netbible.org translator's notes (the NET page I opened had only the Bible text), anything from bibleodyssey.org, and any prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on this passage. Those parts of section 3 are left out.
- **Not verified:** The church labels I give for some writers (Gill as Baptist, Wesley and Clarke as Methodist, Calvin and the Geneva notes as Reformed) come from StudyLight's own tags. I couldn't confirm a church label for every commentator.

---

## 1. Traditional reading, verse by verse

**v. 1**
- **Why Joseph rose:** Ellicott says it wasn't through statecraft, military skill or luck, but "by the direct intervention of Providence." He compares Daniel rising in Babylon by explaining Nebuchadnezzar's dream. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/41-1.htm
- **When the "two full years" start:** Gill, Jamieson-Fausset-Brown, the Pulpit Commentary and the Cambridge Bible all think the count most likely starts when the cupbearer was released (Cambridge says from the baker's execution), not when Joseph went to prison. Clarke reads the phrase as two complete years. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/41-1.htm ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/clarke/genesis/41.htm
- **The wait:** Matthew Henry says we need waiting patience, not just bearing patience. God's time for delivering his people will come, and it will prove to have been the best time. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Gen/Gen_041.cfm
- Guzik (Enduring Word) says God sets both the starts and the stops of his people. When the time was right, the cupbearer knew exactly where to find Joseph. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-41/
- The Expositor's Bible says these quiet years matured Joseph's character, and that his calm, dignified bearing before Pharaoh grew out of them. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/genesis/41.htm
- **Who this Pharaoh was:** Ellicott and the Pulpit Commentary list several options, including Apophis, a "Shepherd" king, and Amenemhat III, which Canon Cook preferred. They treat the question as open. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/41-1.htm
- **"The river":** Ellicott says the Hebrew word is the Egyptian word for "great river," the Bible's usual name for the Nile. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/41-1.htm

**v. 2**
- Barnes says the word for "reeds" means the marsh grass on the Nile's banks. He notes that the cow was the Egyptian emblem of fruitfulness, a hieroglyphic symbol of the earth and farming, and the form in which the goddess Isis was worshipped. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/41-1.htm
- Deffinbaugh (Bible.org) calls the dreams "remarkably Egyptian." Cows cooling off in the Nile and grazing on marsh grass were a typical Egyptian sight. https://bible.org/seriespage/41-pit-palace-genesis-411-57

**vv. 3–4**
- Deffinbaugh says the puzzle was that cows don't eat cows, and the lean ones should have grown fat. Something was clearly wrong. https://bible.org/seriespage/41-pit-palace-genesis-411-57
- Clarke says both kinds of cattle could fitly come out of the same river, because the Nile's flood could be full, partial or held back. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/clarke/genesis/41.htm

**vv. 5–6**
- **The second dream:** Barnes says the repetition was meant to confirm the warning, as Joseph later explains in v. 32. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/41-1.htm
- **The east wind:** Barnes says it could mean any wind from the east side, and the scorching wind in Egypt usually blows from the southeast. Keil and Delitzsch identify it as the Chamsin, the southeast wind off the Arabian desert. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/41-1.htm

**v. 7**
- Barnes says the dream felt so real that Pharaoh took it for reality until he woke up. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/41-1.htm
- Guzik says it was a strange, lifelike dream, but also a message from God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-41/

**v. 8**
- **Pharaoh troubled:** Guzik says Pharaoh sensed in his spirit that the dream mattered. The interpretation belonged to God, who didn't give it to Egypt's magicians. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-41/
- Matthew Henry says the dreams carried their own evidence that God sent them, so Pharaoh was rightly troubled. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Gen/Gen_041.cfm
- **Who the magicians were:** Barnes says they were sacred scribes from the priestly class who also read the stars and interpreted dreams. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/41-1.htm
- Deffinbaugh says they were Egypt's best-educated men, trained in dream interpretation. They failed because the dreams were God's revelation, which can only be grasped through his Spirit (1 Cor 2:10–16). https://bible.org/seriespage/41-pit-palace-genesis-411-57
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says that, unlike Babylon's wise men, they didn't even pretend to know the meaning. God left them stumped so Joseph's inspired wisdom would stand out. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Gen/Gen_041.cfm

**vv. 9–13**
- **What the cupbearer's "failures" were:** see section 2, where commentators disagree.
- Barnes notes that the phrase "a Hebrew lad" shows the Egyptians knew the Hebrew people even when Israel was only one family. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/41-25.html
- Deffinbaugh points out that the cupbearer never mentions that Joseph was jailed unjustly. He also says nothing of Joseph's character or faith, only his skill. https://bible.org/seriespage/41-pit-palace-genesis-411-57
- Matthew Henry (concise) says God's timing was best. If Joseph had been freed earlier he might have gone home and missed becoming a blessing to his family. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/41-16.htm

**v. 14**
- **"Quickly brought":** the Pulpit Commentary and Gill say the Hebrew literally means they "made him run." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/41-14.htm
- **"Dungeon":** Poole and Benson take the word loosely for the prison as a whole. Joseph was probably no longer kept in the pit itself, since he was running the prison. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/41-14.htm
- **Shaving:** Barnes and Jamieson-Fausset-Brown say Egyptians shaved their heads and beards except when in mourning. Ellicott adds that Egyptian monuments show only captives and low-ranking men with beards. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/41-14.htm
- Deffinbaugh calls the shave "a cultural concession." Hebrews saw a beard as dignified, but Egyptians found it offensive, so Joseph shaved to avoid offending the king. https://bible.org/seriespage/41-pit-palace-genesis-411-57
- Ellicott cites the Jewish commentator Abravanel: each of Joseph's sufferings was matched by a reward. He was hated for dreams and raised up by dreams, stripped of his coat and then clothed in fine linen, thrown into a pit and then drawn out of the prison-pit. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/41-14.htm

**v. 15**
- Keil and Delitzsch explain Pharaoh's words as "you only need to hear a dream and you can interpret it at once." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/41-16.htm
- The Expositor's Bible says Pharaoh had a revelation from God he couldn't read: one man gets the revelation, another the interpretation. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/genesis/41.htm
- Guzik compares Pharaoh to someone who reads the Bible but needs a godly person's help to understand it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-41/

**v. 16**
- Guzik says Pharaoh offered Joseph a chance to glorify himself, and Joseph refused. He seems humbler than when he told his brothers his own dreams. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-41/
- **"Not I":** Barnes says Joseph habitually credits his gift to God. The Cambridge Bible says God's servant may be his spokesman, but "is not as God, nor is he a magician." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/41-16.htm
- **"A sound answer":** the Pulpit Commentary says the Hebrew literally means God "shall answer the peace of Pharaoh," that is, what will be for Pharaoh's welfare. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/41-16.htm
- Deffinbaugh notes that Joseph never mentions his own release. His first concern was God's glory, not his own comfort. https://bible.org/seriespage/41-pit-palace-genesis-411-57

**vv. 17–24**
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says the dreams were thoroughly Egyptian. Egypt's fertility depended on the Nile, and oxen in hieroglyphs stood for the earth and food. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Gen/Gen_041.cfm
- **v. 21:** Guzik says the second telling adds detail: the thin cows didn't get fatter after eating. Barnes explains "devoured them" as "into their stomachs." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-41/ ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/41-14.htm
- **v. 24:** Deffinbaugh notes that Pharaoh ends by admitting his best advisers had nothing to say. https://bible.org/seriespage/41-pit-palace-genesis-411-57

**v. 25**
- **"One and the same":** Gill says the two dreams used different images but had one meaning, so one interpretation served for both. Only God knows the future, and those he chooses to tell. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/41-25.htm
- The Pulpit Commentary says the magicians' failure was the best proof that Joseph spoke by inspiration. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/41-25.htm
- **God and the Nile:** Clarke says that although the Nile normally causes plenty or want, its floods are under God's direction. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/41-25.html
- **God over Pharaoh:** Constable notes that Egyptians saw Pharaoh as a god in human form. By accepting the interpretation, Pharaoh put himself under Joseph's God. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/41-25.html
- Barnes says "God" here (literally "the God") means the one true God, as opposed to false gods. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/41-25.html

**vv. 26–27**
- Keil and Delitzsch say the fat cows and ears mean very fertile years, and the lean ones very barren years. The famine would wipe out every trace of the good years. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/41-25.htm
- Coffman says the key was knowing what the number seven stood for: years, not daughters or provinces. The dream also applied to Egypt, not just to Pharaoh. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/41-25.html
- Deffinbaugh says Joseph's interpretation followed the dreams closely in detail, which made it more believable to Pharaoh. https://bible.org/seriespage/41-pit-palace-genesis-411-57

**v. 28**
- Coffman says Joseph's thinking was always God-centred. Here he stresses God's mercy in warning Pharaoh. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/41-25.html
- Guzik says God gave Pharaoh guidance through Joseph. The doubled dream (looking ahead to v. 32) showed both how certain and how urgent the message was. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-41/
- The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary says that in interpreting the dream Joseph shows himself "a true prophet of the Lord." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/genesis-41.html

## 2. Where Protestant commentators differ

**v. 16, "God will give Pharaoh an answer of peace": is it a promise or a wish?** This is the clearest split I found.
- **Calvin (Reformed):** Joseph didn't yet know what the dream meant, so as a prophet he couldn't promise a good outcome. The words are "a prayer rather than a prophecy," spoken out of kindness to the king. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/41-16.html
- **Gill (Baptist, Calvinist):** mentions the reading "may God give…" but prefers to take it as a statement of Joseph's faith that God would answer. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/41-16.htm
- **Wesley (Methodist):** Joseph gives honour to God and shows goodwill to Pharaoh, and "Those that consult God's oracles may expect an answer of peace." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/41-16.html
- **Clarke (Methodist):** reads it as "independently of me." Joseph isn't needed for Pharaoh's comfort, because God has Pharaoh in his care and he will prosper however bad the dreams look. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/41-16.html
- **Poole:** allows "may God give" and reads it as Joseph's wish for a happy answer. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/41-16.htm

**v. 9, the cupbearer's "failures":** This is a disagreement between individual commentators, not a church-by-church split.
- Guzik (Calvary Chapel) says the cupbearer was confessing his wrong against Joseph. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-41/
- Barnes and Deffinbaugh say he meant his earlier offence against Pharaoh. Forgetting Joseph probably didn't even strike him as a sin. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/41-25.html ; https://bible.org/seriespage/41-pit-palace-genesis-411-57

**Reformed Geneva Bible notes:**
- On v. 1: the dream was less for Pharaoh than a way to free Joseph and provide for God's Church. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/41-1.htm
- On v. 14: "The wicked seek the prophets of God in their time of need," while despising them when things go well. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/41-14.htm

**v. 14, Calvin on the shave:** Calvin guessed that Egyptians wore their hair long, so the shave meant Joseph had lain "in filth" until the day he was freed. His own editor says this guess is wrong, citing Herodotus and the monuments. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/41-14.html

## 3. Other views

**Modern scholarship (v. 14):** The Cambridge Bible, quoted on Bible Hub, thinks the clause about the dungeon was added to harmonise two source versions. In the source scholars call "E," Joseph is a slave. In the one they call "J," he is a prisoner. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/41-14.htm

**Reading Joseph as a picture of Christ (v. 14):** This is popular devotional teaching, not one of the views you listed.
- Bible Hub's study notes say Joseph's release foreshadows the Exodus and Christ's resurrection, and his change of clothes pictures putting on the new self (Eph 4:22–24). https://biblehub.com/genesis/41-14.htm
- They also say the scene "prefigures Christ's role as the mediator." https://biblehub.com/study/genesis/41-14.htm

**Coffman (Churches of Christ) on v. 25:** He applies "the dream is one" to the Book of Revelation. In his view, Revelation's seven judgment scenes are seven views of one final judgment, not seven separate judgments. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/41-25.html
